newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Eurosceptic Swedes warm to link to Europe.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Eurosceptic Swedes warm to link to Europe.

text.p: Like Britons reluctant to create a land-link to France, Swedes and Danes have hardly been clamouring for a bridge and tunnel between their countries.

Environmental concerns -- rather than any unease about their neighbours -- have fuelled controversy over the scheme, approved in 1991, which will be Sweden's first link to the rest of continental Europe.
But opinion polls are starting to show more people backing the plan than opposing it, even among Swedes, who recently topped the list of most reluctant European Union nations.

"It is the first time we have had more people for the project overall," spokesman Leif-Goran Persson told Reuters in Malmo, where the Swedish part of the project starts. "We think the tide has turned."

By late 2000, the 16km (10 mile) construction over the Oresund Strait should halve journey times between Sweden's third largest city and the Danish capital Copenhagen, cutting the trip to just 25 minutes from around an hour now.
The $2.3 billion project, funded 50/50 by Sweden and Denmark through the companies Svedab and A/S Oresundsforbindelsen, will be even quicker than catamaran or helicopter connections.
ENVIRONMENTAL SOLUTIONS
The cities' 2.3 million residents seem ready to accept that the eight-km (five-mile) bridge section need not seriously affect the water flow to the Baltic Sea, damaging marine life.
The Oresund Consortium has developed what it calls a "zero solution", pledging the water flow will be reduced by only 0.5 percent.
Spillage from dredging must not exceed five percent on average and work will halt if levels rise too much.
With these hurdles overcome, recent protests have focused not on the environment but on less specific, if still typically Scandinavian, concerns.
Stop The Bridge activists have chained themselves to equipment at various sites to demonstrate against the "undemocratic way" in which they say the project was approved.

Still, the most recent bi-annual opinion poll showed -- in Sweden -- less polarised views: 36 percent of those questioned were in favour of the project with 36 percent opposed, down from 38 percent for and 39 percent against in the last poll.
In Denmark, respondents were being won over: 35 percent of interviewees supported the link, 33 percent against.
In both cases the rest were undecided.
"Residents of southern Sweden have always been for the bridge but northern Swedes have always said they do not want it," said Leif-Goran Persson.
"They do not see the need for it and do not want the cost. It has nothing to do with national sentiment."
TOLLS TO FUND PROJECT
Though funded from state coffers, the project will be repaid through tolls from the estimated 10,000 cars a day expected to use it.
The Oresund Consortium, with an AAA Standard & Poor's credit rating, has raised money on capital markets but aims to repay its debts within 26 years of the bridge opening.
The Oresund link will allow Swedes to go from Malmo into Denmark and the international airport Kastrup and then cross the bridges linking Denmark's main islands to the continent.
Work on building the columns and bases for the bridge has already started and first pillars will be in place in April.
The Oresund consortium has contracted three consortiums to carry out the work.
The dredging group, Oresund Marine Joint Venture, involves Great Lakes Dredge & Dock Co of the U.S., Ballast Nedam Dredging b.v. of Holland and Per Aarsleff AS.
Sundlink Contractors HB, responsible for the bridge, includes Sweden's Skanska AB, Denmark's Hojgaard & Schultz A/S and Monberg & Thorsen A/S, and Hochtief AG of Germany.

Oresund Tunnel Contractors, who are building the tunnel, involves Sweden's NCC, the Laing Group from Britain, Boskalis Westminster Dredging BV of the Netherlands, Dumez-GTM of France and E.Pihl & Son AS.
Either side of the Oresund, Denmark and Sweden are preparing road and rail connections for the link.
But Persson said the project was viewed primarily as of regional benefit -- and would benefit Sweden more than Denmark.
"This is still very much a regional affair. Connections to Germany will still be mainly by ferry," he said.
"It has greater significance and economic value for Sweden than Denmark."
